name: Gareth Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a drummer, and my year splits roughly in half. Half the time I'm the house drummer at Foundry Lane Studios, playing on pop records, adverts and the odd film. The other half I tour with an indie pop band called Paper Harbour, mostly theatres and festivals. A studio day is ten till six with a lot of coffee; a tour day is a van, a soundcheck and ninety minutes of going flat out.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Touring is more fun, the studio pays more reliably. I like knowing that on a Tuesday I'll be at Foundry Lane with Marcus, the engineer, and we'll get three songs done. Ten years of drumming has taught me that a steady Tuesday is worth more than a great Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Drum machines have been around since before I was born and drummers still work. I'd make a joke about it in the band chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably very little changes. The studio already uses software to tighten timing and sometimes to replace a kick drum sound. That keeps happening, but they still book me to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep both halves of the job going. Pay off the last bit of my mortgage a bit faster, since I'm already close. Maybe buy a vintage snare I've had my eye on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a good life and it stays a good life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How close are you to paying off the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four years left at the current rate, three if I push. I bought a small flat when I was twenty-four with money from a big tour. Owning my flat at thirty would mean a quiet month of gigs never frightens me again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anyone at Foundry Lane you'd worry about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe the junior engineers, because a lot of their editing work is the routine stuff software already does. Marcus is too good to be bothered.

I'd make a **joke** about it in the band chat.
think: The studio keeps using software to **tighten timing**, but still books me.
**Very little** changes in my working week.
do: Keep both **studio and touring** work going as now.
Pay off the last of the **mortgage** a year faster and maybe buy a vintage snare.
feel: **Calm**: it's a good life and it stays that way.
S0.quote: Owning my flat at thirty would mean a quiet month of gigs never frightens me again.
fieldNote: Gareth's **split income** between studio and touring makes him feel balanced.
Owning his **flat** outright is his main financial goal.
He sees **junior engineers**, not himself, as the ones nibbled at.

steps.text: Keep house drumming at Foundry Lane and touring with Paper Harbour
Overpay the mortgage to clear it a year early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and musicians should be honest about it. Session work is going to change. I'd say that to younger drummers too, not to scare them, just so they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my studio half takes the hit. If a producer can get a decent, human-sounding drum track from software in minutes, they won't book me for every advert. They'll still want me for the records that need feel, but that's maybe a third of what I do there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take more touring work, maybe a second band, to make up the difference. I'd learn the drum software properly, because if I can program a good part and play over it, I'm more useful to producers. And I'd hold off on the vintage snare and keep paying the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be counting my studio days every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many studio days a month now, and what would you expect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About ten now. In this picture I'd guess six within two years. Going from ten studio days to six is the difference between a comfortable year and a careful one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is touring a real fallback? It's hard on the body.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I'm only twenty-seven, so I've got some years of vans and floors in me. I wouldn't want to do it at forty. But for now it's the safest part of my job.

I'd tell **younger drummers** straight, not to scare them.
think: I think my **studio half** takes the hit, especially adverts.
Producers will still want me for records needing **feel**, maybe a third of studio work.
do: Add a **second touring band** to replace lost studio days.
Learn the **drum software** properly to program and play over parts.
Delay the **vintage snare** and keep paying the mortgage.
S1.quote: Going from ten studio days to six is the difference between a comfortable year and a careful one.
fieldNote: Gareth expects studio days to drop from **ten to six**, a real income cut.
He'd meet it by **leaning into touring**, which is hands-on and safer.
As a steady adopter, he'd learn software once he sees **producers using it**.

steps.text: Join a second touring band to fill lost studio days
Learn the studio's drum programming software properly
Skip the vintage snare purchase this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody needs to think about the people caught in it. I'm not one for big political statements, but I'd say that much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the studio work disappears within a year of 2028. Every advert, every pop record could have perfect drums for nothing. Touring holds until robots come around 2031, and even then I'm not sure people want a robot drummer, but ticket sales would drop if everyone's losing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the mortgage completely in the first year using savings, so my costs are tiny. I'd tour as much as my body can handle. I'd also start teaching drums, because a kid learning in a room with a real kit needs a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lose half my income almost overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Paying off the mortgage uses your cushion. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a trade. No mortgage means I can live on very little. I'd rather have no mortgage and an empty savings account than a full account and a monthly bill I can't pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marcus, the engineer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what he's planning. He's forty-five with two kids, so it's worse for him. Maybe we'd teach together, him on recording, me on drums.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and someone must think about people caught in it.
I'm not one for **big political statements**, but I'd say that much.
think: I think **studio work** disappears within a year of 2028.
**Touring** holds until robots, but ticket sales drop if people lose jobs.
do: Clear the **mortgage** in year one using savings, to shrink fixed costs.
Tour as much as his **body** can handle.
feel: **Alarmed** at losing half his income almost overnight.
S2.quote: I'd rather have no mortgage and an empty savings account than a full account and a monthly bill I can't pay.
fieldNote: Gareth expects to **lose half** his income fast, which makes this alarming despite savings.
His plan is to **cut fixed costs** to almost nothing by clearing the mortgage.
He thinks of **Marcus**, older with kids, as worse off.

steps.text: Use savings to pay off the flat mortgage in full
Tour with Paper Harbour and a second band as much as possible
Start teaching children drums face to face on a real kit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years and we should plan. I'd talk to other drummers about it honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio side still goes, around 2030. But five years gives me time to build teaching up properly before that, and to finish the mortgage on schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start teaching two evenings a week now, building a list of students. I'd keep touring and the studio while they last. I'd also take a short course in sound engineering, so I can record other bands myself if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel I was ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sound engineering, when that's also thinking work AI could take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair. I suppose because live sound is hands-on, setting up mics in a real room. Live sound at a small venue is something a drummer already half knows, and it needs someone standing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your plans about where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd stay. Plenty of music work around here, and the flat's nearly mine.

S3.quote: Live sound at a small venue is something a drummer already half knows, and it needs someone standing there.
fieldNote: Five years lets Gareth build **teaching** before studio work falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and I'd plan sensibly. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd naturally be touring less by then anyway. I'd be thirty-seven, mortgage gone, probably teaching more. The studio work would fade gradually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do for now. Pay off the flat on time. Start teaching one evening a week in a few years and grow it slowly. Learn the drum software when the producers I work with start using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you uneasy if the plan is fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That studio drumming might simply stop being a job for anyone. I'd be fine with ten years of warning, but the kid who wants to be a session drummer today probably wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell that kid not to try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd tell them to learn to teach and play live too, so they're not relying on the studio.

I'd keep it **low-key**, nothing dramatic, at work or online.
think: By **thirty-seven** I'd be touring less anyway, mortgage gone, teaching more.
**Studio work** would fade gradually rather than all at once.
do: Pay off the **flat** on schedule and keep current work.
Start **teaching** one evening a week in a few years and grow slowly.
Learn the **drum software** once his producers use it.
S4.quote: I'd be fine with ten years of warning, but the kid who wants to be a session drummer today probably wouldn't.
fieldNote: With a decade, the change fits Gareth's **natural career arc** away from touring.
His unease is for **future drummers**, more than himself.
He'd adopt software **when proven** among his producers.

steps.text: Keep the studio and touring split and clear the mortgage on time
Learn drum programming software once Foundry Lane producers use it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because half my income would go before I could build anything else. What would help is a few years of transition money for session players, and maybe funding for music teaching in schools so there are jobs to move into.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the body. Drummers have a shelf life for touring. If the studio goes, a lot of us are left with only the part of the job that wears you out fastest.

headlineQuote: Ten years of drumming has taught me that a steady Tuesday is worth more than a great Saturday.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old** drummer who splits his year between studio sessions and touring.
He's **pragmatic** and steady, adopting tools once he sees producers using them.
He expects AI to hit his **studio half** hard, leaving touring and teaching.
His key move is to clear the **mortgage** so his costs are tiny.
He worries touring is the part of the job that **wears the body** fastest.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because half his income goes before he can build alternatives.
whatWouldHelp: **Transition money** for session players and funding for school music teaching.
